about.title: Light, passed from lamp to lamp
about.p1: Deepotsav (दीपोत्सव) means “festival of lamps”. Deepavali (दीपावली), or Diwali, means “a row of lamps”. It falls on Amavasya, the new-moon night, the darkest of the lunar month, usually in October or November.
about.p2: Hindus, Jains and Sikhs, and many Buddhists in Nepal, each keep it for their own reasons. Keep scrolling: this journey follows those stories.
about.explore: Explore as you go. Unlit diyas are waiting for your touch, five small things are hidden around the courtyard, and there is a blessing for today. Your journal keeps track of everything you find.
story1.title: Fourteen years
story1.p: In the Ramayana, Prince Rama of Ayodhya accepts fourteen years of exile in the forest so that his father, King Dasharatha, can keep a promise he once made. Sita and Rama’s brother Lakshmana choose to go with him.
story2.title: Light over darkness
story2.p: During the exile, Sita is abducted by Ravana, king of Lanka. With Hanuman and an army of allies, Rama crosses the sea, and after a long war Ravana is defeated. Many communities mark that victory as Dussehra, about twenty days before Diwali.
story3.title: The road to Ayodhya
story3.p: Once the exile is over, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana travel home. In Valmiki’s telling they ride the flying chariot Pushpaka. Hanuman goes ahead with the news to Bharata, who has ruled in Rama’s name all those years with Rama’s sandals on the throne.
story4.title: A city of lamps
story4.p: Tradition holds that the people of Ayodhya lit clay lamps along every path, rooftop and riverbank to welcome them home on that moonless night. Deepavali remembers that welcome. In Ayodhya today, millions of diyas are lit for Deepotsav on the banks of the Sarayu.
story4.aside: The Ramayana is told in hundreds of versions across South and Southeast Asia, and families link Diwali to different stories. Some of those stories follow.
lakshmi.title: Welcoming Lakshmi
lakshmi.p1: On the evening of Amavasya, families worship Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, good fortune and well-being. She is usually worshipped together with Ganesha, who removes obstacles. In one well-known story, Lakshmi rose from the churning of the cosmic ocean.
lakshmi.p2: Homes are cleaned and left open to the light. Rangoli is drawn at the threshold, often with small footprints leading inside to welcome the goddess, and lamps are kept burning into the night. In western India many business families begin a new financial year at this time, and bless their new account books in Chopda Pujan.
dhanteras.title: Dhanteras
dhanteras.p1: Dhanteras (Dhanatrayodashi) opens the five days of Diwali. Its name joins dhan, wealth, and teras, the thirteenth day of the waning moon, two days before Lakshmi Puja.
dhanteras.p2: The physician of the gods. When the devas and asuras churned the cosmic ocean (the Samudra Manthan), Dhanvantari rose from the waters carrying a pot of amrita, the nectar of immortality. He is the physician of the gods and the deity of Ayurveda. Dhanteras is also kept as Dhanvantari Jayanti, a day to pray for good health, in the spirit of the saying “पहला सुख निरोगी काया”: the first happiness is a healthy body.
dhanteras.p3: The lamp that kept Yama away. A popular legend tells of King Hima’s son, whose stars foretold death by snakebite on the fourth night of his marriage. That night his young bride heaped her gold and silver ornaments and coins at the door, lit lamps all around, and kept him awake with stories and songs. Yama, god of death, came in the form of a serpent, but the blaze of light dazzled him. He sat on the glittering heap listening until dawn, then quietly went away.
dhanteras.p4: So on Dhanteras many families light a lamp for Yama (Yama Deepam) outside the home, facing south, the direction of Yama. They buy something new in gold, silver or metal, often utensils, and worship Lakshmi and Kubera, keeper of the treasures of the gods. At the threshold of the courtyard you can see a heap of gold and a four-wick lamp, one wick turned to the south.
jain.title: The nirvana of Mahavira
jain.p1: For Jains, Diwali marks the nirvana (moksha) of Bhagwan Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara. According to Jain tradition he attained it at Pavapuri, in present-day Bihar, in 527 BCE.
jain.p2: The Kalpa Sutra says the assembled kings lit lamps that night: since the light of knowledge had gone, they would make a light of material things. The next day his chief disciple, Gautama Swami, attained kevala jnana (omniscience), and the Jain new year, Vira Nirvana Samvat, begins.
jain.p3: Many Jains keep the day with fasting, prayer and recitation of the Uttaradhyayana Sutra, believed to be Mahavira’s final teaching. Many also choose lamps over firecrackers out of ahimsa, care for every living being.
sikh.title: Bandi Chhor Divas
sikh.p1: Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the “Day of Liberation”. In 1619 (sources differ slightly on the year), the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, was freed from Gwalior Fort, where Emperor Jahangir had held him.
sikh.p2: The Guru refused to leave unless 52 imprisoned kings were freed with him. He was told that only those who could hold on to his robe might go, so he had a cloak made with 52 tassels, and every one of them walked out with him.
sikh.p3: When he reached Amritsar, the Harmandir Sahib was lit with lamps. It still is: every year the Golden Temple and its sarovar shine, and gurdwaras around the world gather in celebration.
days.title: Five days of light
days.d1: Dhanteras: Dhanvantari and Lakshmi are honoured; buying metal is auspicious, and a lamp is lit for Yama.
days.d2: Naraka Chaturdashi (Choti Diwali): Krishna’s victory over the demon Narakasura. In the South, Maharashtra and Goa the day starts before dawn with an oil bath. In Tamil Nadu, this is Deepavali itself.
days.d3: Lakshmi Puja: the new-moon night of lamps, rangoli and sweets shared with neighbours. In Bengal, Assam and Odisha, Kali Puja is celebrated on this same night.
days.d4: Govardhan Puja · Bali Pratipada · New Year: Krishna lifting Govardhan hill to shelter the people of Braj, with temples offering Annakut, a “mountain of food”. In Maharashtra and Karnataka, the generous King Bali is remembered, couples celebrate Padwa, and Gujarati families welcome the New Year (Bestu Varas).
days.d5: Bhai Dooj: sisters pray for their brothers’ well-being and brothers give gifts. It is Bhau-beej in Maharashtra, Bhai Phonta in Bengal and Bhai Tika in Nepal.
days.aside: Days follow the lunar calendar, and customs differ from region to region and family to family.
regions.eyebrow: III · Across India and the world
regions.title: One festival, many lights
regions.r1: Bengal, Assam, Odisha: Kali Puja on Amavasya. In Odisha, families burn jute sticks in Kaunria Kathi to light the way for ancestors.
regions.r2: Gujarat: Chopda Pujan for the new accounts, then the New Year with greetings of Saal Mubarak.
regions.r3: Maharashtra: trays of faral sweets and snacks, and clay forts built by children in memory of Shivaji’s forts.
regions.r4: Goa: giant Narakasura effigies paraded and burned before dawn.
regions.r5: Tamil Nadu: a dawn oil bath, new clothes and the greeting “Ganga snanam aacha?”, meaning “Have you had your Ganga bath?”
regions.r6: Punjab: Bandi Chhor Divas at the Harmandir Sahib.
regions.r7: Nepal: Tihar, five days honouring crows, dogs, cows and Lakshmi, Mha Puja among the Newars, and Bhai Tika.
regions.r8: Varanasi: fifteen days later, on Kartik Purnima, the ghats glow again for Dev Deepawali.
regions.r9: Around the world: a public holiday in Fiji, Guyana, Malaysia, Mauritius, Nepal, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Suriname and Trinidad and Tobago, and celebrated in cities from Leicester to Durban and Toronto.
rangoli.title: Draw at the threshold
rangoli.p: Rangoli welcomes guests, and on Diwali Lakshmi, at the door. The design on the courtyard floor is yours to redraw: mirrored symmetry, powder colours, petals and dots.
fw.title: Paint the sky
fw.help: Tap the sky to launch. Choose the sparkler and drag across the sky to write with light. Made only of light, with no smoke, and no sound unless you turn it on.
fw.fine: Many cities limit firecrackers to protect air quality, animals and people who are sensitive to noise. Light as many of these as you like.
wish.title: Set a wish afloat
wish.p: On Diwali, and again on Kartik Purnima, diyas are set afloat on rivers, lakes and the sea. Write a wish and send your diya out across the water. Tap a floating diya of yours to read its wish.
wish.label: Your wish
wish.placeholder: May everyone I love be well…
wish.consent: Also share this wish anonymously on the public wish wall
wish.consentFine: Off unless you tick it. Only the wish text is sent: no name and no device details.
wish.done: Your diya is on the water. Tap it in the river any time to read your wish again.
wish.privacy: Your wishes stay on this device. Nothing is uploaded.
greet.title: Your Diwali greeting
greet.fine: The names and message travel only inside the link or image you share. Nothing is stored on a server. Opening the link shows them a diya to light, and then your message.
end.title: May your light reach every home
end.thanks: Thank you for lighting a diya with us.

studio.help: Draw with a finger, pen or mouse. With the keyboard: arrow keys move the brush, hold Shift to move faster, Space toggles drawing, Enter places a stamp or ring, plus and minus change the size, and Control+Z undoes. Escape closes the studio.
set.motionNote: Reduced motion replaces camera flights with gentle fades.
set.install: Install Deepotsav to open it like an app, even offline.
set.privacyText: No accounts, no analytics, no tracking. Your rangoli and wishes are saved only in this browser. Greetings travel only inside the links or images you choose to share.
set.keyboardText: Scroll with the arrow keys, Page Up / Page Down or Space. Every control can be reached with Tab.

hunt.owl.name: Lakshmi’s owl
hunt.owl.riddle: Lakshmi’s companion sees best at night. Look high up, where the lamps climb towards the sky.
hunt.owl.story: Lakshmi is often shown with an owl, the ulooka. An owl sees clearly in the dark, a reminder to stay wise and awake even when fortune shines. In Bengal, an owl seen on the night of Lakshmi Puja is thought to be lucky.
hunt.mouse.name: Ganesha’s mouse
hunt.mouse.riddle: Someone very small has found the sweets beside the Dhanteras gold.
hunt.mouse.story: Ganesha rides a mouse, Mushika. Lakshmi and Ganesha are worshipped together on Diwali night, so wherever there is gold and a laddoo, his little friend is never far away. It is a reminder that even the smallest creature can carry great wisdom.
hunt.peacock.name: The peacock
hunt.peacock.riddle: A bird with a hundred eyes stands guard at the far end of the pool.
hunt.peacock.story: India’s national bird carries Kartikeya, Ganesha’s brother, and its feather crowns Krishna. Peacocks fill countless rangolis, and a peacock dancing at the first rain is a sign of good things to come.
hunt.cow.name: The sacred cow
hunt.cow.riddle: A gentle guest rests beside the lamp tower, honoured on the day before Dhanteras.
hunt.cow.story: On Vasu Baras, the day before Dhanteras, many families in Maharashtra and Gujarat honour cows and their calves. Two days after Lakshmi Puja, Govardhan Puja remembers Krishna, the young cowherd, lifting a whole hill to shelter the cows and people of Braj.
hunt.conch.name: The conch
hunt.conch.riddle: Something white and spiral floats where the first diya came to rest.
hunt.conch.story: The shankha, a conch shell, is blown at the start of a puja, and its sound is said to clear away negativity. Like Lakshmi, it is said to have risen from the churning of the cosmic ocean, and Vishnu holds one in his hand.
bless.1: May your home be full of light, and your heart lighter still.
bless.2: A diya loses nothing by lighting another. May your kindness keep spreading.
bless.3: May Lakshmi find your door open and your home happy.
bless.4: May every road you take this year be lit, even the long ones.
bless.5: Tamaso ma jyotirgamaya: lead me from darkness to light.
bless.6: The first happiness is a healthy body. May you have plenty of it.
bless.7: May the sweets be many and the arguments few.
bless.8: One flame can light a thousand lamps. Be someone’s first flame today.
bless.9: May your worries burn out faster than a phuljhadi.
bless.10: May Ganesha clear the obstacles before you even see them.
bless.11: Clean the corners of your home and of your mind, and let the light reach both.
bless.12: May you have the patience of the bride who kept the lamps burning all night.
bless.13: May every “Saal Mubarak” you hear this year come true.
bless.14: A row of lamps is stronger than one. May your people always stand with you.
bless.15: May you come home, as Rama did, to people who kept the lights on for you.
bless.16: Light that is shared is never halved. Share yours freely.
bless.17: May the rangoli of your days be colourful, balanced and only a little smudged.
bless.18: Like the kings who held on to the Guru’s cloak, may you never walk out of hard times alone.
bless.19: May knowledge be the brightest lamp in your house.
bless.20: May the new year open like a fresh account book, with every line in your favour.
bless.21: Light a lamp tonight for someone far away. They will feel it.
bless.22: May your sky be full of colour and your air free of smoke.
bless.23: Even the darkest night of the month becomes the brightest night of the year. Hope is like that.
bless.24: May you be the reason someone smiles at their window tonight.
